To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

SARS CoVs are not only capable of inducing IFN, but also of inhibiting it, depending on their genetic and protein composition, and that this inhibition is mediated by the viral protein N and the host protein STAT1.

SARS CoVs are a family of RNA viruses with a single positive stranded genome that encode for 16 proteins, including a spike (S) protein, an envelope (E) protein, a nucleocapsid (N) protein, a membrane (M) protein, an accessory protein (3a) and a replicase polyprotein (1ab).
SARS CoVs, SARS CoVs 1, 2 and MERS, are highly similar in their host immune responses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of IFN in COVID 19 infection and the role of IFNs as potential therapeutics.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms that regulate cytokine production in monocytes and macrophages.
identifying the mechanisms by which the innate immune system is activated in response to SARS CoV infection, and to identify novel targets for therapeutic intervention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

COVID 19 infection is characterized by the release of pro inflammatory monocyte associated chemotactic cytokines, which are likely to be responsible for the cytokine storm observed in severe cases of COVID 19.
the immune response in COVID 19 is similar to the immune response in other viral respiratory infections, and the severity of COVID 19 is associated with the severity of the immune response.
SARS Co V2 is a highly infectious virus, and its pathophysiology is driven by a strong inflammatory response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cytokine response is the main driver of COVID 19 pathogenesis.

the cytokine response to SARS CoV2 infection is similar to that of SARS CoV1, MERS CoV and IAV infection, but not to HPIV3 or RSV (Wang et al. 2004; Zaki et al. 1985; Zaki etal. 2004) The cytokine response in COVID 19 patients is also distinct from the cytokine response seen in influenza A virus infection.

the cytokine storm in SARS CoV infection is mainly driven by the innate immune system, and the adaptive immune system is not involved in the cytokine storm, which is in contrast to the cytokine storm of influenza infection (Wang et al. 2004) In contrast, a recent study showed that the adaptive immune system, specifically CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, is also involved in the cytokines storm in SARS (Wang et a. 2010)
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single chemokine or cytokine that is responsible for the pathogenicity of SARS CoV2.
SARS CoVs are not unique in inducing monocyte activation, but rather, this is a shared feature of all beta coronaviruses (de Wit et. al., 2020; Amanat & Krammer, 2020).
the IFN response is not the main target of SARS CoV2 infection.
